title: Checking in at a homestay
setting: A family-run homestay in Ubud, Bali, early in the afternoon. You come in through the garden gate with your backpack, and the owner, a woman in her fifties, comes out to meet you.

n1.speaker: host
n1.indonesian: Selamat siang. Ada yang bisa saya bantu?
n1.english: Good afternoon. Can I help you?

options.feedback: Atas nama gives the name on the booking. If you booked through an app, add lewat aplikasi.

options.indonesian: Selamat siang, Bu. Saya Sam. Saya sudah pesan kamar.
options.english: Good afternoon. I'm Sam. I've booked a room.
options.feedback: Returning her greeting, with Bu, is a warm start. Sudah pesan (have already booked) is how people say they have a booking.
Correct, but stiff and translated from English. People say Saya sudah pesan kamar, literally 'I've already ordered a room'.

n2.speaker: host
n2.indonesian: Oh, iya. Selamat datang, Kak. Boleh pinjam paspornya sebentar?
n2.english: Ah, yes. Welcome. Could I borrow your passport for a moment?

options.feedback: Ini … saya works for anything you hand over. Every place you stay will note your passport details.
Boleh answers a Boleh …? question: yes, you may.

options.english: Why borrow it? There's no need.
options.feedback: Pinjam (borrow) is just the polite way to ask: she'll note the details and hand it straight back. It's normal everywhere you stay.

n3.speaker: host
n3.indonesian: Terima kasih. Ini kuncinya, Kak. Kamar nomor tiga, di atas.
n3.english: Thank you. Here's your key. Room three, upstairs.

options.feedback: Worth asking on arrival. Termasuk means included.
Sarapannya (the breakfast) plus jam berapa? asks the time of anything.

options.indonesian: Apakah sarapan termasuk dalam harga kamar?
options.english: Is breakfast included in the room price?
options.feedback: Correct, but it sounds like a form: apakah and dalam harga kamar belong in writing. Sudah termasuk sarapan? is what people say.

n4.speaker: host
n4.indonesian: Iya, Kak. Sarapannya jam tujuh sampai jam sepuluh, di teras.
n4.english: Yes. Breakfast is from seven till ten, on the veranda.

options.feedback: Password is the everyday word, and -nya on Wi-Fi-nya makes it 'the Wi-Fi' here.
Ada …? (is there …?) works for anything you need: air panas, handuk, Wi-Fi.
Understood, but Anda sounds stiff face to face, and it isn't really her own password. Use -nya for 'the': Password Wi-Fi-nya apa?

n5.speaker: host
n5.indonesian: Password-nya ada di kartu di meja kamar. Kalau perlu apa-apa, panggil saya saja, ya.
n5.english: The password's on a card on the table in your room. If you need anything, just call me.

options.feedback: Baik (fine, all right) acknowledges what she said, and terima kasih banyak thanks her warmly.
Right everywhere, with anyone. Add Bu to make it warmer: Terima kasih, Bu.
Bye-bye is for friends and children, not someone you call Ibu. Terima kasih, Bu is what fits here.

end.speaker: narration
end.english: Checked in. Handing over your passport is normal wherever you stay. On arrival, ask the things you'll need: Sudah termasuk sarapan?, Sarapannya jam berapa? and Password Wi-Fi-nya apa? At a family homestay you'll see the same host every day, so learn her name: Bu plus her name is warm and polite.
